extracted.intended_audience: scholars, historians and philosophers of science, and scientists interested in the nature of scientific practice and discovery
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing scientific discovery and paradigm change
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for how scientific research proceeds under paradigms, how discoveries arise (anomaly, assimilation), and when paradigm change is necessitated. Useful for evaluating historical cases of discovery and for understanding methodological constraints on normal science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms guide research by modeling more than rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradigms guide research primarily by providing concrete models and exemplars of previous achievements rather than by explicit, abstracted rules; scientists learn what to do largely through exposure to these paradigm applications rather than by articulating rules of the game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that many scientists can describe particular hypotheses but are 'little better than laymen at characterizing the established bases of their field'; paradigms therefore have priority over any explicit rules and function as the primary organizers of normal research practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal science is puzzle-solving and does not aim at novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal science is the puzzle-solving activity that steadily extends scope and precision of knowledge but does not aim at novelties of fact or theory; when successful it finds none.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although normal science does not aim to produce surprises, it nonetheless can and does produce unsuspected phenomena; this explains how work under paradigms can lead, inadvertently, to discoveries that require paradigm change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery begins with awareness of anomaly
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery commences with the awareness of anomaly — the recognition that nature has somehow violated the paradigm-induced expectations that govern normal science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition of anomaly is the essential first step; after that comes exploration of the anomalous area and eventual theoretical adjustment so that the anomalous becomes expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery is an extended process of observation and conceptual assimilation
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery is not a single instant but a process that includes both observational recognition and the gradual conceptual assimilation that makes the phenomenon intelligible within scientific categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assimilation closes only when the paradigm theory has been adjusted; examples (oxygen, X-rays, Leyden jar) show discovery involves experimentation, reinterpretation, and gradual acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of a discovery depends on degree of violation of paradigm expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The value placed upon a new phenomenon and thus upon its discoverer varies with the extent to which the phenomenon violated paradigm-induced anticipations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A phenomenon that deeply conflicts with entrenched expectations is more likely to precipitate crisis and be judged highly significant (e.g., oxygen vs. routine element discovery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority and dating of discoveries are often arbitrary and misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about who 'discovered' something and exactly when are often inappropriate because discovery is a process involving recognition and conceptualization, not a single act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority disputes (e.g., Priestley vs Lavoisier vs Scheele) are symptomatic of a misleading image of discovery as instantaneous; dating must be treated with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization produces multiple, non-coextensive paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: Different professional subspecialties may acquire different paradigms or different applications of a shared paradigm; a change affecting one tradition may be revolutionary for that subgroup but not for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: physicist vs chemist views of a helium atom; quantum mechanics can mean different things to practitioners depending on training, texts, and journals they follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrumental procedures and standard tests embody expectations and can blind researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard experimental procedures and tests are derived from prior experience and carry implicit expectations that can prevent researchers from recognizing phenomena that behave outside those expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: the standard 'goodness of air' test led Priestley and Lavoisier to misidentify oxygen; standard chemical tests delayed recognition of fission products. Paradigm procedures thus restrict the phenomena accessible at any time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discoveries have multiple pathways: accidental, theory-induced, or anticipated
rubrics_metrics.description: Discoveries can arise by accident (X-rays), by speculative/theory-induced investigation (Leyden jar), or as anticipated results of normal-science projects (e.g., predicted chemical elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different origin types influence how quickly and in what way a discovery is assimilated into science and whether it precipitates paradigm change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some discoveries necessitate paradigm change in procedures and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: A discovery can require revision of both theoretical categories and experimental procedures/ instrumentation — not only new theory but also changed laboratory practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: X-rays necessitated shielding of apparatus and re-evaluation of previous experimental results; discoveries can thereby change what counts as proper instrumentation and control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigms function without explicit rationalization until they are insecure
rubrics_metrics.description: While paradigms remain secure they can function without agreement over rationalization or any attempted rationalization; debates about rules, methods, and standards arise when paradigms are felt to be insecure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-paradigm periods and revolutionary crises are marked by frequent and deep debates over legitimate methods, problems, and standards of solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anomalies lead to crises and debates about legitimate methods and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: When paradigms are attacked by anomalies, debates recur about the nature and standards of the field — these debates define schools and can precipitate paradigm change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical transitions (e.g., Newtonian to quantum mechanics) evoked disputes about standards of physics; such debates are regular markers of peri-revolutionary periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptual and psychological factors influence recognition of anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological processes can make anomalous stimuli difficult to recognize; experimental evidence (Bruner and Postman playing-card experiment) suggests perception itself is shaped by expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cognitive constraints help explain why anomalous phenomena can go unnoticed until conceptual categories change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior awareness of theoretical difficulty predisposes to discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance sense that existing theory is inadequate can enable some investigators to see in experiments what others do not; being prepared to discover is often crucial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lavoisier had earlier recorded discontent with phlogiston theory; his prior awareness allowed him to interpret Priestley’s results differently and to synthesize the oxygen theory of combustion.
